keyVerseText: When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay, anointed: or, spread the clay upon the eyes of the blind man
rootMeaning: The Greek noun πτύσμα (ptýsma) derives from the verb πτύω (ptýō), meaning 'to spit.' This etymology highlights its literal sense as something produced by the act of spitting—namely, saliva or spittle. Understanding πτύσμα as the physical substance expelled by spitting adds a vivid, tangible dimension beyond the simple English gloss 'spittle,' emphasizing its bodily and somewhat humble nature.
usageInScripture: The word πτύσμα appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in John 9:6, where it is translated as 'the spittle.' This singular occurrence points to a very particular and focused usage, tied to the physical act of Jesus using his saliva to create clay for healing. The consistency of its translation underlines the concrete, material reality of the term, without metaphorical extension in Scripture.
theologicalSignificance: The original meaning of πτύσμα as 'spittle' invites reflection on the incarnational and tangible aspects of Christ's ministry. Jesus' use of spittle to heal the blind man underscores how God can use ordinary, even lowly elements of human life to accomplish divine purposes. It also points to the intimate and personal nature of Jesus' healing power—He does not operate from a distance but engages with the physical world and human frailty. This reminds believers that God's grace often comes through simple, accessible means, demonstrating His humility and the profound sanctification of the material world through Christ.
keyVerseReflection: In John 9:6, the text states, 'When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay.' The word πτύσμα here emphasizes the physical reality of Jesus' healing act, showing that He used His own saliva as part of the healing process. This detail highlights the personal involvement of Christ in the miracle and enriches our understanding of His incarnational approach to restoration.
